subject: chiton mollusc
title: This Sea Creature Sees Through Hundreds of Eyes Made of Rock

scenes.text: This animal's eyes are made of rock. Hundreds of them.
It's a chiton, a mollusc that clings to tropical shores under a coat of armour plates.
Those plates are dotted with hundreds of tiny eyes, each less than a tenth of a millimetre across, and every lens is aragonite, the same mineral as the shell.
In 2011, biologists at Duke and Santa Barbara tested them: hold a dark disc over a chiton and it clamps down on the rock. A disc just three centimetres wide set it off.
In 2015, a team at MIT showed the rock lenses focus real images, in air and underwater. Armour that sees.
So next time you pry one off a rock, remember: it saw you coming.

description:
A chiton's eyes are made of rock: hundreds of tiny lenses of aragonite, the same mineral its armoured shell is built from.
The West Indian fuzzy chiton (Acanthopleura granulata) carries hundreds of eye-like structures, each less than a tenth of a millimetre across, embedded in its shell plates. In 2011 Daniel Speiser and Sonke Johnsen (UC Santa Barbara and Duke) showed in Current Biology that the animals react to dark discs as small as 3 cm passing overhead, and that the lenses work both in air and underwater. In 2015 an MIT-led team reported in Science that the aragonite lenses form focused images.
What other animal would you never have guessed could see?
thumbnail_text: HUNDREDS OF EYES MADE OF ROCK
first_comment: Lenses of stone, hundreds of them, on an animal most people have never heard of. Would you rather have one great eye or 500 tiny ones?
